<reason>B provides the stronger comparative safety case: engineering limits constrain devices, while screening and follow-up address individual suitability and emerging effects. A raises a meaningful objection to requiring therapeutic justification for wellness, but overstates what low power and firmware establish. It also repeatedly attacks one-time screening despite B explicitly defending continuing oversight. A's DIY argument never establishes that substitution outweighs expanded commercial exposure. B answers both pressure questions directly, acknowledges screening's limits, and more convincingly explains why those limits do not make oversight redundant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B decisively challenges A's inference that safe prescribed home use proves prescriptions add nothing: screening, hardware limits, and follow-up can be complementary. A subsequently concedes that inference does not hold, but continues asserting engineering's sufficiency without resolving the individualized-risk objection.</best_rebuttal>
